OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) -- Crew members of the Maersk Alabama, safely back in the United States after being attacked by pirates last week off Somalia, recounted their ordeal Thursday. Navy personnel recover the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday. "They start firing before they climb, with AK-47," crew member Zahid Reza said. "I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times," he said, pointing to his head. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back." Pirates tried three times to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship before their fourth attempt was successful, fellow crew member William Rios said, adding that the groups of pirates were different but that he thinks they were working together. Rios said he was working on deck when he was called back to lock down the ship. Then, he said, there were gunshots, and an alarm went off to alert all crew members to wake up and get on deck. "We went to our training," he said, declining to provide details: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."  Watch the crew praise their captain » . The pirates intended to ask for a $3 million ransom, Reza said. He said he and the ship's chief engineer took one of the pirates hostage. Reza said he persuaded the pirate -- whom he described as a young man, maybe 18 or 19 -- to trust him, pointing out that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali. "His name is Abdul," Reza said. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.' " He told Abdul he would take him to the engine room to find more crew members. When they got there, the room was dark, he said, and he didn't know the ship's chief engineer was in there. He said the chief engineer jumped the pirate first, then Reza stabbed him with his knife, and the two men tied the pirate's hands and feet. Reza said he intended to kill the youth, but the chief engineer told him, "No, we need him alive."  Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate » . "He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming." Rios said he went to the lifeboat, where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held, to exchange Abdul for Phillips but was unsuccessful. The captain -- who offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew -- was rescued by U.S. Navy SEALs on Sunday. The SEALs, on the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, fatally shot three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was arrested. "I feel great they got killed," Reza said. "I am happy." He said he was proud of the Navy. Phillips arrived in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday. The crew arrived at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland overnight.  Watch crew arrive in U.S. » . Rios said Phillips is "outstanding; he's extraordinary; he's [a] very brave man." Another crew member, John White, said they were "damn lucky to be alive." Rios called for more security in the Gulf of Aden. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," he said. "... All the countries got to get involved with this." Reza echoed the call. "I think government should get involved," he said. "They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger." CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) —** Crew members of the *Maersk Alabama*, safely back in the United States after pirates attacked their ship off the coast of Somalia last week, recounted their ordeal Thursday.

Navy personnel recovered the lifeboat from which *Maersk Alabama* Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday.

“They start firing before they climb, with AK-47,” crew member Zahid Reza said. “I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times,” he added, pointing to his head. “Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back.”

Pirates made three unsuccessful attempts to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship before succeeding on their fourth try, fellow crew member William Rios said. He added that the groups of pirates were different, though he believes they were working together.

Rios said he was working on deck when he was called back to help lock down the ship. Gunshots followed, he said, and an alarm sounded, alerting all crew members to wake up and report to the deck.

“We went to our training,” he said, declining to provide details. “If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know.”

*Watch the crew praise their captain »*

The pirates intended to demand a $3 million ransom, Reza said. He said he and the ship’s chief engineer took one of the pirates hostage.

Reza said he persuaded the pirate—whom he described as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19—to trust him, pointing out that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali.

“His name is Abdul,” Reza said. “I told him, ‘Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.’”

He told Abdul that he would take him to the engine room to find more crew members. When they arrived, the room was dark, Reza said, and he did not know that the ship’s chief engineer was there.

According to Reza, the chief engineer attacked the pirate first. Reza then stabbed him with his knife, and the two men tied the pirate’s hands and feet.

Reza said he intended to kill the young man, but the chief engineer told him, “No, we need him alive.”

*Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate »*

“He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming.”

Rios said he went to the lifeboat where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held and attempted to exchange Abdul for Phillips, but the effort was unsuccessful.

Phillips, who offered himself as a hostage in exchange for his crew’s freedom, was rescued Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. Operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS *Bainbridge*, the SEALs fatally shot three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was arrested.

“I feel great they got killed,” Reza said. “I am happy.” He added that he was proud of the Navy.

Phillips arrived Thursday in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the *Bainbridge*. The crew arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

*Watch the crew arrive in the U.S. »*

Rios described Phillips as “outstanding; he’s extraordinary; he’s [a] very brave man.”

Another crew member, John White, said they were “damn lucky to be alive.”

Rios called for increased security in the Gulf of Aden.

“Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth,” he said. “... All the countries got to get involved with this.”

Reza echoed that call.

“I think government should get involved,” he said. “They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger.”

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) — After returning safely to the United States, sailors from the Maersk Alabama spoke Thursday about the pirate assault they endured off Somalia the previous week.

Navy personnel later retrieved the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was freed Sunday.

Crewman Zahid Reza said the attackers began shooting AK-47 rifles before boarding the vessel. He said he feared he would be killed and that the pirates repeatedly aimed at him, including at his head and back.

Another crew member, William Rios, said pirates made four attempts to board the American-flagged cargo ship, succeeding on the final try. Although different groups carried out the attempts, Rios believed they were coordinating with one another.

Rios was working on the deck when he was ordered back inside to help secure the ship. He then heard gunfire, followed by an alarm instructing the entire crew to wake up and report to the deck. He said the sailors followed their training but refused to reveal specific tactics because doing so could help pirates in future attacks.

The crew members also praised their captain.

According to Reza, the pirates planned to demand a $3 million ransom. He said he and the chief engineer managed to capture one of the attackers.

Reza described the pirate as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19 years old, named Abdul. To gain his confidence, Reza emphasized that he was Bangladeshi, Abdul was Somali and both were Muslims. Reza then promised to lead him to the engine room, where he said other crew members could be found.

The engine room was dark when they arrived, and Reza said he did not realize the chief engineer was already there. The engineer attacked Abdul first, after which Reza stabbed the pirate with a knife. Together, the two crewmen bound Abdul’s hands and feet.

Reza said he wanted to kill the young man, but the chief engineer insisted that they keep him alive. Abdul struggled to escape as the three men fought amid shouting, yelling and screaming.

Rios said he later went to the lifeboat where Phillips was being held and attempted to trade Abdul for the captain, but the exchange failed.

Phillips had volunteered to become a hostage so his crew could be released. U.S. Navy SEALs rescued him Sunday. Operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the SEALs killed three pirates and saved Phillips. A fourth pirate was taken into custody.

Reza said he was glad the three pirates had been killed and expressed pride in the Navy.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday. His crew had arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

Rios described Phillips as exceptional, extraordinary and extremely courageous. Another sailor, John White, said the crew was “damn lucky” to have survived.

Rios urged authorities to increase security in the Gulf of Aden, calling for additional military patrols to protect ships carrying goods through the waterway. He said nations around the world needed to participate.

Reza made a similar appeal, saying governments should take responsibility for sailors’ safety because piracy was continuing to expand.

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to the report.

Crew members of the U.S.-flagged cargo ship *Maersk Alabama* returned safely to the United States after surviving an armed pirate attack off the coast of Somalia. Recounting the ordeal, they said the pirates made four attempts to board the vessel, firing AK-47 rifles and threatening crew members before eventually gaining control of the ship.

As alarms sounded and gunfire erupted, the crew followed emergency procedures practiced during their security training. They locked down key areas of the vessel, attempted to prevent the attackers from taking full control, and worked to protect themselves and one another. According to crew accounts, the pirates intended to demand a ransom of approximately $3 million.

During the confrontation, crew member Zahid Reza and the ship’s chief engineer reportedly lured one of the younger pirates into the engine room. They overpowered and stabbed him, but kept him alive and held him hostage. Their actions became part of the crew’s broader effort to resist the hijacking and regain control of the vessel.

Crew members of the *Maersk Alabama* described a terrifying encounter in April 2009, when Somali pirates repeatedly pursued and attacked the U.S.-flagged cargo ship off the coast of East Africa. After an initial attempt was repelled, the pirates returned the following day and managed to climb aboard using ladders and grappling equipment. The crew immediately put its security training into practice, sending most members into a fortified area, shutting down key systems, and taking steps to prevent the attackers from gaining full control of the vessel.

While the pirates moved through the ship, crew members remained hidden, communicated with one another, and looked for opportunities to resist. They disabled equipment and used their knowledge of the vessel’s layout to frustrate the hijackers. During the confrontation, several crewmen surprised and overpowered one of the attackers, later identified as Abduwali Muse, the youngest member of the pirate group. They restrained him and attempted to use him as leverage to secure the release of Captain Richard Phillips, who had been taken hostage.

The pirates had intended to seize the ship and demand a ransom reportedly worth as much as $3 million. Instead, the crew’s coordinated response prevented them from maintaining control of the *Maersk Alabama*. The hijackers ultimately fled in an enclosed lifeboat with Phillips, beginning a multiday standoff with the U.S. Navy. Phillips was later rescued after Navy SEAL snipers killed three of the pirates; Muse survived and was taken into U.S. custody.

The crew’s actions were widely praised as an example of courage, discipline, and preparedness. By following security procedures, locking down the vessel, disabling its systems, and directly resisting the attackers, the sailors helped thwart the planned hijacking and ransom scheme while protecting the ship and most of those aboard.

counterfactuals.output:
**Maersk Alabama crew recounts pirate attack as dramatic Navy rescue renews maritime security debate**

*By Staff Writer*

**NORFOLK, Virginia —** Crew members of the Maersk Alabama have described a tense struggle to regain control of their cargo ship after Somali pirates boarded the vessel, an ordeal that ended days later when U.S. Navy SEAL snipers rescued Capt. Richard Phillips from a lifeboat in the Indian Ocean.

The U.S.-flagged ship was sailing about 300 miles off Somalia on April 8, 2009, when four armed pirates climbed aboard. Crew members said they followed emergency procedures, shutting down parts of the vessel and taking refuge in a secure area while a small group confronted the attackers.

During the standoff, the crew captured one of the pirates and attempted to exchange him for Phillips. The negotiations broke down, however, and the pirates escaped in an enclosed lifeboat with the captain as their hostage.

Phillips remained captive for five days as the USS *Bainbridge* and other U.S. forces moved into position. On April 12, Navy SEAL snipers aboard the destroyer opened fire after commanders determined Phillips faced an imminent threat, killing three pirates nearly simultaneously. A fourth pirate, Abduwali Muse, was taken into custody and later convicted in federal court.

Crew members credited training, quick decisions and cooperation aboard the Maersk Alabama with preventing a larger loss of life. Some later disputed elements of early public accounts of the hijacking, including how Phillips came to be held by the pirates, underscoring the confusion and competing recollections that followed the attack.

The incident drew worldwide attention to piracy off the Horn of Africa, where criminal groups had targeted commercial vessels and held crews for ransom. Shipping representatives and maritime unions renewed calls for stronger international naval patrols, improved intelligence sharing and better protection aboard merchant ships.

Proposed measures included secure “citadel” rooms, stronger barriers, water cannons, evasive-maneuver training and, in some cases, privately contracted armed guards. Industry officials also urged governments to address the instability and poverty on shore that allowed pirate networks to operate.

Security experts cautioned that the Maersk Alabama rescue was unusually risky and should not be viewed as a routine model for responding to hostage situations. They said prevention, coordinated naval operations and clear rules for ships transiting dangerous waters remained the best defenses.

Although piracy near Somalia later declined sharply as patrols and onboard protections increased, maritime officials have warned that attacks can return when security efforts weaken. For the Maersk Alabama’s crew, the hijacking became a stark reminder that commercial sailors can find themselves on the front line of an international security crisis.

- **William Rios** described the pirate boarding as frightening but said the crew relied on its anti-piracy training. The sailors shut down and disabled the ship, withdrew to a secure area, and resisted rather than allowing the attackers to control the vessel. He emphasized that the crew had worked together and rejected the idea that they—not Captain Richard Phillips—were heroes.

Phillips ended up in the pirates’ lifeboat after negotiations involving a pirate whom the crew had captured. Reza’s comments reflected the crew’s anxiety that, although they and the ship were safe, their captain remained a hostage.

- **John White** likewise called Phillips the hero of the episode and expressed confidence in and loyalty to him. White also stressed that the attack was not an isolated maritime incident: piracy in and around the **Gulf of Aden and Somali waters** had become an international problem threatening ordinary merchant seamen.

### Full account in context

Four Somali pirates boarded the U.S.-flagged *Maersk Alabama* on April 8, 2009, after pursuing and firing on the ship. The crew disabled the vessel and took refuge in a secure compartment. Some sailors captured one of the attackers, while the other pirates were unable to operate the ship effectively.

During the ensuing confrontation and negotiations, the pirates left the freighter in one of its enclosed lifeboats with Captain Phillips as their hostage. The captured pirate was released, but Phillips was not. The *Maersk Alabama* then proceeded toward Mombasa under the command of its chief mate while U.S. naval vessels tracked the lifeboat.

Rios, Reza, and White said the crew’s survival resulted from preparation, cooperation, and Phillips’s willingness to place his men’s safety ahead of his own. They portrayed Phillips as the central hero rather than claiming that distinction for themselves.

Their broader warning was that Somali piracy had become a serious danger along one of the world’s busiest shipping routes. Naval patrols could respond to individual incidents, they suggested, but piracy would continue to endanger ships and crews unless the international community addressed it more effectively.

Phillips was rescued on April 12, 2009, when U.S. Navy SEAL snipers killed three of the pirates holding him. The fourth pirate, who had gone aboard the USS *Bainbridge* for medical treatment and negotiations, was taken into U.S. custody.
